extracted.intended_audience: people seeking cultural competence about Australia (travelers, expatriates, HR/training/educators)
extracted.subtask_description: An overview of salient Australian cultural values, behaviours and social norms intended to help readers understand how Australians commonly relate to one another and the world. Useful for intercultural training, travel preparation, workplace diversity awareness, and general education about Australia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mateship
rubrics_metrics.description: Australian friendships run deep and are especially loyal; it is common for people to rely upon their friends or ‘mates’ in hard times more than family. Migrants and foreigners are often surprised by how openly and quickly Australians begin to establish the basis for this mateship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Relationships tend to be built on camaraderie rather than hierarchy; respect is shown through gestures of equality instead of deference. It is considered bad taste to ask someone to do anything you would not do yourself. ‘Dobbing’ (reporting misdemeanours to authorities) is seen as unacceptable. People who knowingly put mates in awkward situations are disliked. Use of the term implies deep loyalty and mutual fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Egalitarianism
rubrics_metrics.description: Egalitarianism strongly underpins interpersonal values in Australia. People believe in the right to a ‘fair go’ regardless of background; Australia is often described as a classless society where privilege is seen as being 'better off' rather than 'better than'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Level of education and wealth does not necessarily earn status or respect; casual clothing and similar accents across classes exemplify this. Sociologists tie this dismissal of stratification to Australia’s transition from penal society. Anti-patterns: overt displays of superiority, arrogant behaviour, and clear attempts to elevate oneself above peers may provoke resentment (tall poppy syndrome). Note that social divisions do exist for marginalised groups and increasing market competitiveness can produce stratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern Australian society asserts a confident and unique identity through diversity, language(s), architecture, 'Australianised' cuisine, bush identity and sporting prowess.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authenticity is expressed by adapting cultural roots to local environment and resources. Being perceived as 'down-to-earth' and straightforward is valued; simplicity is endearing. Anti-patterns include appearing pretentious or overly 'cultured', which can invite suspicion or resentment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Optimism
rubrics_metrics.description: Many Australians enjoy a high standard of living and a reasonably optimistic outlook on freedom and possibilities; a common national narrative hails Australia as the ‘lucky country’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surveys find a majority believe Australia has the best lifestyle; despite this optimism, Australians resist overt displays of national superiority. Expect general confidence tempered by modesty about accomplishments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humility / Self-deprecation
rubrics_metrics.description: Australians are often very modest about their accomplishments and commonly self-deprecate to avoid seeming pretentious. Leaders and awardees may downplay status to appeal to the ‘true-blue Aussie’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humility is essential; people who show arrogance or achievement above peers are often 'cut down' (tall poppy syndrome). Examples: refusals of national awards, leaders downplaying socio-economic status. Anti-patterns: boasting, overt self-promotion, or ostentatious displays of superiority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Informality
rubrics_metrics.description: Australians favour informality in social interactions; gestures of equality and casual behaviour are common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Casual clothing is typical even among affluent Australians; social interaction prioritises fairness and equality over deference. Formal displays of rank or status are less effective socially. In workplaces and day-to-day contexts, expect relaxed forms of address and low hierarchical signalling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Easy-going / Relaxed approach
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a cultural tendency toward a relaxed approach; people often respond with 'she’ll be right' and avoid putting themselves under pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise relaxation, holidays and winding-down. Procrastination and avoidance of excessive worrying are common; people who exert themselves visibly (eagerness, impatience, stress) may be seen as exasperating. However, this relaxed attitude coexists with strict enforcement of certain laws (safety regulations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Common sense / Simplicity
rubrics_metrics.description: Simplicity and common-sense reasoning are valued; being perceived as 'down-to-earth' and straightforward is an endearing quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Being called a 'classic' is a compliment among friends. Practical, straightforward solutions and plain speaking are positively regarded. Anti-patterns: appearing overly intellectual or 'cultured' without approachability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour (larrikinism and irreverence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour is a central component of Australian culture, often expressing a light disregard for authority (larrikinism) and employing self-deprecation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Australian humour celebrates underdog characters and irreverence toward rules; it can be used to deflate pretension. Expect teasing, sarcasm, and a tendency to mock arrogance. Caution: humour that is perceived as punching down or insensitive to historical injustices (e.g., Indigenous experiences) may be offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules and Relaxation (contradictory norms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Australians express a light disregard for authority in attitudes and humour, yet are conscientious about following the rule of law; society contains many practical regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: cyclists can be fined heavily for not wearing helmets even though society is stereotyped as laid-back. Some Australians call strict enforcement 'Nanny state'. Expect this tension: informal attitudes in social life coexisting with stringent public safety and regulatory enforcement. Avoid assuming lawlessness from relaxed demeanour; follow local regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander experiences and diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: The Indigenous people and nations of Australia are the traditional custodians of the land (estimated 60,000 years). There were at least 250 distinct language groups prior to colonisation; colonisation caused violence, dispossession and drastic population decline and ongoing marginalisation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat Indigenous culture as homogenous; recognise diverse traditions, spiritualities and customs. Understand the continuing custodial relationship to land and the trauma of colonisation; reconciliation and formal recognition remain important issues. Advice: consult Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultural resources and courses for sensitive referencing. Avoid minimising or discounting historical injustices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiculturalism in Australia
rubrics_metrics.description: While the mainstream has generally adopted Anglo/Celtic-Western customs, Australia is increasingly multicultural due to immigration from Asia, Africa and the Americas; in 2016 roughly 26% were born overseas and 49% had at least one parent born overseas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most Australians accept multiculturalism and view it as the country's future; younger generations increasingly see bi-cultural identities as assets. Be aware, however, of reactionary attitudes in national politics and debates around immigration. In everyday life Australians generally treat people of all backgrounds equally, though political discourse can differ.
